hops.title: Compare it: a sandcastle bucket is a mold
hops.text: A sandcastle bucket helps. The hollow bucket is a mold, and the castle that slides out is a cast. In nature, a shell buried in mud can dissolve and leave a hollow mold, and mud can fill it to make a cast. Ammonites were sea animals that usually had coiled shells. The biggest is about as tall as a grown-up.

hops.title: Ask it: what can a footprint tell us?
hops.text: While you press toy animal feet into clay, ask, "If we only saw these tracks, what could we guess?" Your child might count toes, guess size, or count how many animals walked by. Cheer every clue. In Alaska's Denali National Park, rocky "dinosaur dance floors" packed with tracks even hint that young and grown-up dinosaurs traveled together.

sources.citation: U.S. National Park Service, Denali National Park and Preserve: Trace Fossils

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: Large and small three-toed dinosaur footprints preserved in a flat gray rock slope.
image.caption: Fossil footprint trails help scientists spot toe shapes, size, and young animals traveling with a grown one.

hops.title: Point at it: sea fossils in stone walls and steps
hops.text: On your next walk, stop beside pale limestone steps, park walls or museum blocks. Look closely for tiny stone rings, little five-sided stars and curved shell outlines. Some of those rings may be pieces of crinoid stalks. Crinoids are sea animals nicknamed "sea lilies," and crinoid-rich limestone was used to build the Capitol Reflecting Pool in Washington, D.C.

sources.citation: U.S. National Park Service, Fossil Echinoderms: Crinoids, Blastoids, and Others

image.caption: Limestone walls and steps can hide real fossil rings and stars from ancient sea animals.

audio.title: Three easy ways to talk about fossil prints
audio.transcript:
Pressing shells into clay is the fun part, and a few easy tips can turn it into a real conversation. Here are three to try.

First, before you use the words mold and cast, grab something your child already knows: a sandcastle bucket. The hollow bucket is the mold. The bumpy castle that slides out is the cast. In nature, a shell buried in mud can dissolve and leave a hollow mold, and mud or minerals can fill that mold and harden into a cast. Ammonites were sea animals that usually had coiled shells, and the biggest ammonite fossil ever found is about six feet across, about as tall as a grown-up.

Second, when your child presses toy animal feet into the clay, ask, "If we only saw these tracks, what could we guess?" Let them count toes, guess how big the animal was, or count how many animals walked by. Every idea is a good clue. Real scientists play this game too. In Denali National Park in Alaska, rocks packed with dinosaur tracks are nicknamed dinosaur dance floors, and some tracks even hint that young and grown-up dinosaurs traveled together.

Third, take the hunt outside. On your next walk together, stop by pale stone steps or a stone wall and look closely. Tiny stone rings and little five-sided stars may be fossils. Some of those rings may be pieces of crinoid stalks. Crinoids are sea animals nicknamed sea lilies. Crinoid-rich limestone was even used to build the Capitol Reflecting Pool in Washington, D C.

Have fun, and enjoy every wild guess along the way.
